definition: The visual cycle is the light-driven process in vision in which retinal, the light-sensitive part of rhodopsin, changes from an 11-cis form to a trans form and triggers a shape change that starts visual signaling. Enzyme-catalyzed, energy-requiring reactions then convert it back to the cis form so the system can be used again.

provenance.scope: Source record D012172; pinned source text

reasons: The packet describes retinal/retinaldehyde as the active component of the visual cycle, not the visual cycle itself, so the definition uses the wrong sense of the term.

The opening claim that the visual cycle is the light-driven process in vision is not directly supported by the packet; the packet only states that visible light converts 11-cis-retinal to 11-trans-retinal as part of rhodopsin’s response.
The definition is more expansive than the packet and turns a descriptor entry for a molecule into a definition of the entire visual cycle.

The definition states that “retinal” is “the light-sensitive part of rhodopsin”; the packet describes 11-cis-retinal as the prosthetic group of rhodopsin and the active component of the visual cycle, but does not explicitly call it “the light-sensitive part.”
The definition says the shape change “starts visual signaling”; the packet says the shape change “trigger[s] the visual process,” but does not explicitly support the term “visual signaling.”

The clause “so the system can be used again” is not explicitly stated or directly supported; the packet only says energy-requiring enzyme-catalyzed reactions convert 11-trans-retinal back to the cis form.
